cards.text: Last chapter of Leviticus, friend, and the LORD has more to say to Moses, Israel's leader. He tells Moses to speak to the Israelites about this: what happens when someone makes a special vow to the LORD involving the value of persons.

Then comes a price list in silver, set by age and by male or female, from one month old to sixty and older. If the one making the vow is too poor to pay, the priest sets the value by what he can afford. Friend, Mother Miller bought me out of a closing bakery's bin for 25 CENTS. And that price INCLUDED the mustache.
Next up: animals. Somebody vows an animal that may be brought as an offering to the LORD.

cards.question: Any animal fit to be an offering that's vowed to the LORD shall be ___.
Once an offering animal is vowed to the LORD, the owner must not swap it for another, good for bad or bad for good.

cards.text: If the owner swaps anyway, both animals become holy. An unclean animal, one that can't be brought as an offering, goes before the priest, who sets its value. To buy it back, the owner adds a fifth, and friend, keep your eye on that fifth, because it's about to become a THEME.

Now a man consecrates his house as holy to the LORD, and the priest values it, good or bad. That price STANDS, friend, so no running after the priest yelling, "Wait, you didn't see it after I dusted!" To get the house back, he adds a fifth to its value, and it's his again.

Now fields. A man's own land is valued by the seed it takes, and the price drops when fewer years are left until the next Year of Jubilee. Buying it back costs a fifth more, and friend, the fifth is BACK, like an oven timer I swear I already turned off. If he never buys it back, or sells it, it belongs to the priests once it's released in the Jubilee. A man who consecrates a field he bought pays its value that day as a sacred offering, and in the Jubilee it goes back to its original owner.
Every value uses the sanctuary shekel, twenty gerahs to the shekel. Then comes a firstborn of the livestock, an ox or a sheep, and nobody may consecrate one.

cards.question: Why can't anyone consecrate a firstborn ox or sheep to the LORD?

answers.text: It already belongs to the LORD
It is too young to be offered
It belongs to the oldest son

cards.text: If that firstborn is an unclean animal, the owner can buy it back by adding a fifth. If he doesn't, it's sold.
Now take something a man sets apart to the LORD from all he owns, whether a man, an animal or his inherited land. Everything so devoted is most holy to the LORD.

cards.question: A man can buy back something he devoted to the LORD by adding a fifth to its value.

cards.text: This part is heavy, friend. "No person set apart for destruction may be ransomed; he must surely be put to death."
Last topic, friend: the tithe from the land, whether it comes from the seed of the land or the fruit of the trees.

cards.question: The tithe from the land's seed and fruit trees is holy. Who does it belong to?

cards.text: Buying back part of the tithe costs a fifth more. Every tenth animal that passes under the shepherd's rod is holy to the LORD, and the owner must not check whether it's good or bad or swap it. If he swaps anyway, both become holy and neither can be redeemed. Try to game the count, friend, and instead of one animal going to the LORD, it's TWO.

These are the commandments the LORD gave Moses for the Israelites on Mount Sinai. That's the LAST verse of Leviticus, and my cookie cutter kid Ruby is shaped like a bell, so friend, if any line ever deserved a bell, it's that one.
